newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS - FX vols spike up after Greenspan comments.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - FX vols spike up after Greenspan comments.

text.p: Implied volatilities for dollar-pair options spiked up in the U.S. after spot rates rallied on remarks by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan hinting an imminent credit tightening, dealers said.

"Vol sensitivity shifted from the downside to the upside," said Alan Revercomb, options strategist at I.D.E.A. Inc. "We started at the middle and had a vol spike on the early dip...and then Greenspan spoke and effectively hiked rates."
The dollar, after an early slide toward 1.67 marks and 122.00 yen, vaulted above 1.69 marks and 123.50 yen after the Greenspan comments.

Greenspan said in testimony before Congress's Joint Economic Committee that the Federal Open Market Committee, which meets next week, must weigh risks of any policy decision, including leaving rates unchanged.
One-month dollar/mark and dollar/yen implied volatilities rose nearly half a point each from late Wednesday levels to 9.9/10.2 percent and 10.2/10.4 percent respectively.
Volatilities for one-week options, which mature just after next Tuesday's FOMC meeting, shot up over a full point, with dollar/mark at 10.7/11.7 percent and dollar/yen at 10.0/11.0 percent.
While one-week dollar/mark had been firm for a few days, one-week dollar/yen had been relatively subdued, due in part to a market holiday in Tokyo today.

"Yesterday, everyone seemed to be happy with their gamma exposure," said Masao Okada, chief options dealer at Dai-ichi Kangyo Bank in New York. "But there's been enough spot movement to justify holding gamma and FOMC is posing a very big event risk now."
Shorter-dated options have higher gamma, which makes them more sensitive to spot market gyration but vulnerable to time decay.

Revercomb said recent range-trading in the 120-125 yen and 1.67-1.72 mark ranges had caused a build-up of short option positions slightly beyond those levels, either outright in vanilla options or in exotic option barriers.

"It's probably not going to be real sensitive until we get over 1.70 (marks) and 124 (yen), but you get there and you start getting into shooting distance of short-gamma exposure that hasn't been on the radar screens for a while," he said.
"As we get closer to the extremes of these ranges, especially in dollar/yen, it will move interest further out the curve," Revercomb added.

"Certainly, if we take out the highs, it's going to incite more belief that there's going to be volatility down the road," he said. He noted that uncertainty over the fate of a single European currency, Japan's resurgent trade surplus and fragile U.S. asset markets could be a drag for the dollar but could also add to the greenback's volatility.
Risk reversals, the put/call pricing differential, were shifting back toward mark puts and yen puts after being neutral to slightly skewed for calls in the past few days.
One-month 25-delta was around par in dollar/mark and 0.1/0.3 percent in favor of yen puts in dollar/yen.
